soil-env-185.title: Rebuilding soil faster than it is lost
soil-env-185.text: Soil can be made, not only spent. Soil regeneration is the creation of new soil and the restoration of soil health. It means keeping topsoil loss low, holding more carbon than escapes, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working. It is a form of ecological regeneration within restoration ecology, reforming degraded soil through biological, chemical or physical processes. Healthy soil mixes living organisms, organic matter and mineral material, and air and water typically fill half its volume. Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by microbes in the rhizosphere. That bargain keeps the living biomass mostly fungal and raises soil carbon. Carbon is also the best gauge, since organic carbon content is one of the most predictable signs of a degraded soil. Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon and lets the soil recover. For optimal plant growth, the carbon to nitrogen ratio must stay at 20–30:1. A diverse soil life also crowds out disease, because competition shrinks the niche open to parasites. The rewards are carbon stored against climate change, less erosion and a sturdier soil overall.

soil-env-177.title: Testing a soil's health, not just its nutrients
soil-env-177.text: A routine {{ref:soil-fert-187}} asks which nutrients a field holds. Soil health testing asks a broader question: how well does the soil deliver its ecosystem services, judged against benchmarks? It combines physical, chemical and biological analyses. Benchmarks include carbon dioxide release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium. Woods End Laboratories has offered a soil quality package since 1985, and Cornell University a Soil Health Test since 2006. Both combine aggregate stability, mineral balance and CO2 respiration, now seen as hallmarks of the field. Other labs add a respiration test called the CO2-Burst to routine chemical tests. Testing is spreading in the United States, Australia and South Africa. Yet many labs and scientists resist the new biological tests. Fertility metrics rest on crop-response models, and none exist for soil health; critics add that novel tests may miss management changes. Others say the old models, built for maximum yield, have failed. US soils may have lost up to 75% of their carbon over the past 40 years, though that figure is debated. In practice, testing still serves mostly agronomic goals.

soil-env-173.title: Soil science beyond the farm gate
soil-env-173.text: Soil science does not stop at the edge of the field. Environmental soil science studies how people interact with the pedosphere and with the living world, rock, water and air around it. It is one of the general subfields of edaphology, alongside agricultural soil science, and looks beyond crop production. Its topics run from surface water quality, stormwater and erosion control to {{ref:soil-env-195}}, wastewater land treatment and wetland restoration. It covers polluted ground and its cleanup, soil degradation and nutrient management. It tracks viruses and bacteria moving through soil, and {{ref:soil-env-023}}, the use of microbes to break down pollutants. Land use, global warming and acid rain belong to it too, as do human-made soils such as terra preta. Much of its research relies on models. Soil chemistry itself has shifted toward this field, because its knowledge is key to predicting where contaminants in soil end up.

soil-env-176.title: Healthy for whom? The many meanings of soil health
soil-env-176.text: An ecologist and a farmer can disagree about one soil's health. Users weigh a soil's functions differently, so the term only makes sense against the user's aims and the soil's boundaries. Ecological landscape assessment and agronomic goals each claim their own criteria, and a soil may work well ecologically yet serve crops poorly. Benchmarks also shift with a soil's inherited traits and geography. Generically, a healthy soil absorbs and cycles well, sheds clean runoff, keeps carbon and productivity near climatic limits and leaks few nutrients. Unlike soil quality, soil health is never tied to a purpose such as preparing a roadbed.

soil-env-178.title: Measuring how far farmed soil falls short
soil-env-178.text: How healthy should a farmed soil be? In 2020 Maharjan and colleagues proposed an answer: compare it with native land in the same region. The soil health gap is the shortfall between managed soils and that local benchmark. The idea filled a hole. Without site- or region-specific benchmarks, research on how different farm management affects soil health had been limited. Meanwhile, soil's importance for food security, farm ecosystems, the environment and human life had pushed research strongly toward soil health.

soil-env-175.title: Soil health and soil quality: two overlapping ideas
soil-env-175.text: Soil health sounds like the newer idea, but it is the older one. The phrase grew out of European organic and biological farming movements, well before soil quality became a discipline around 1990. Swiss soil biologist Otto Buess's 1978 essay 'The Health of Soil and Plants' still largely defines the field. Soil quality means fitness for a use, such as growing maize or preparing a roadbed. Soil health takes a holistic view of soil as a self-sustaining living system. Soil health has largely replaced the older term, though the two still overlap considerably.

soil-env-218.title: Permaculture: designing farms on nature's model
soil-env-218.text: In 1978 Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined a word for land management and settlement design that copies flourishing natural ecosystems: permaculture. Its three ethics and Holmgren's twelve design principles are widely cited. Practitioners bury wood to hold soil water, a method called Hügelkultur, and use sheet mulching, no-till gardening, keyline design and vermicomposting. Its standing is contested. It has stayed largely isolated from science, and critics call it pseudo-scientific or poorly defined. Yet some 21st-century studies support claims that it improves soil quality and biodiversity. A 2024 review found that it strongly enhances carbon stocks and soil quality.

soil-env-186.title: Four ways a soil wears out
soil-env-186.text: One third of the globe's land has degraded soil, with around 500 million hectares degraded in the tropics and subtropics alone. Poor management wears soil down in four general ways. The first is erosion, in which water runoff or wind carries soil away, typically from bare fields. Excessive tillage, especially ploughing, leaves soil open to the wind. The second is physical degradation, a change in structure that keeps water and air out. Heavy farm vehicles cause it through compaction. Urban construction compacts and seals soil too, which intensifies storm runoff and erosion. The third is chemical degradation: heavy metals or hydrocarbons, acidification, salinization, nutrient leaching, and toxins from mining and waste management. Cities concentrate pollutants that leach into their soils. The fourth is biological degradation, a loss of biological activity. Chemical fertilizer is one cause. It suppresses nitrogen-fixing microbes and raises nitrous oxide emissions. As fertility falls, more fertilizer goes on, a positive feedback loop. Overgrazing strips away plant roots, and with them organic matter and the partnership between plants and soil microbes. The toll includes lost biodiversity, more greenhouse gas emissions and less carbon storage.

soil-env-188.title: Cover crops, compost and the toolkit of soil repair
soil-env-188.text: A field planted with one crop year after year slowly runs down. Monoculture depletes soil carbon and nutrients, because each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients. Regenerative soil practices, many drawn from conservation agriculture, work to reverse that. Cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced disturbance, mulch retention and integrated nutrient management store more carbon and cut fossil fuel use. Permaculture uses mixed, native and perennial crops and avoids tilling, so microbes and roots stay in longer contact. Holistic management, from Allan Savory's work, claims planned grazing can improve soil health and reverse desertification; researchers dispute the desertification claim. Amendments, chosen to suit the soil's current state, lock up toxins, balance pH, add nutrients and encourage soil life. Inorganic ones improve texture and structure and limit heavy-metal availability. Wood ash, ground limestone and red mud are alkaline amendments; gypsum and dredged materials are mineral ones. Organic amendments such as mulch, compost, biochar, manure and biosolids improve biological activity, water permeability and structure. Biosolids are nutrient-rich, so they should be used sparingly.

soil-env-184.title: How soil withstands shocks and recovers
soil-env-184.text: Soils have outlasted an atmosphere without oxygen, the arrival of land plants 420 million years ago and, since the last ice age, long wet, dry and fire periods. Soil resilience is a soil's ability to resist destabilizing influences or recover its healthy state afterward. Strictly, soil resistance is the inherent capacity to withstand disturbance, and resilience is the capacity to recover after it. Time sets the frame. Soil formation takes thousands of years, while humans have depended on and changed soil for only a short while. Parent material and topography are passive soil-forming factors; climate and living things are active ones, and shifts in them amount to environmental change or shock. Resilience is limited by how fast and how far humans change a soil, against the time it needs to recover. Australia shows the cost. Little more than 200 years of European-style farming has brought salinity, acidity, nutrient decline, erosion and structural decline. Open questions remain: should a soil stay constant or settle at a new equilibrium, and how long can it hold out?

soil-env-180.title: Judging soil quality by what can be measured
soil-env-180.text: Soil function itself is hard to measure directly, so scientists measure stand-ins. These soil quality indicators fall into three groups. Physical indicators include texture, bulk density, porosity, water content at saturation, aggregate stability and penetration resistance. Together they show infiltration and the water available to plants. Chemical indicators include soil pH and nutrient levels, and a typical soil test checks only these. Biological indicators reflect organisms such as earthworms, millipedes, centipedes, ants and spiders, which regulate structure, break down contaminants and cycle nutrients. The Soil Management Assessment Framework pulls such readings together, and Germany rates farm soil on its soil value scale, the Bodenwertzahl. Very few monitoring systems give near real-time indicator data, and almost all report only at research level.

soil-env-189.title: Who decides how soil is used
soil-env-189.text: Since December 2013, by a UN General Assembly decision, the world has marked 5 December as a day for soil, an idea soil scientists put forward in 2002. Behind it lies soil governance: the policies, strategies and decisions that nation states and local governments apply to soil use. It differs from soil management, the practices that raise and maintain a soil's fertility, structure and carbon. Governance needs governments, local authorities, industries and citizens to agree on coherent policies that regulate use, avoid conflicts between users and promote sustainable land management. Globally it has taken a farming view, because food insecurity grips the most populated regions. It focuses on how degradation hurts food production, and on conflict between land for settlements and land for farming. It usually sits within land governance, so urban and industrial soils get little attention. Concern over erosion built awareness, making science and technology the link between management and governance. FAO and UNESCO made a global soil map in 1981, and an ISRIC-led consortium is building a new one with GIS and remote sensing.

soil-found-112.title: Healing land after mines, farms and disasters
soil-found-112.text: Reclaiming abandoned US mines is estimated to cost $9.6bn, and Australian mine rehabilitation bonds total $9.49 billion. Land rehabilitation returns damaged land to some degree of its former state after industry, natural disasters or other harm. Mining, farming and forestry often degrade land. In parts of the United States, reclamation means returning disturbed land to an improved state. At mines, crews contour waste dumps against erosion and cap sulfide ore with clay to stop acid forming. Landfills and tailings get a cover of topsoil, or soil and vegetation.

soil-env-187.title: The carbon that farming has pulled from the ground
soil-env-187.text: The top two meters of soil hold an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes of carbon. That is more than the atmosphere's 879 billion and vegetation's 600 billion together. Each year some 61 billion tonnes leave soils as organic carbon decomposes and oxidizes. A similar amount returns through decomposition and plant–microbe symbiosis. Farming and fossil fuel use tip that balance. Since farming began, an estimated 133 billion tonnes of carbon has been lost from soil, mostly in the last two centuries of mechanized agriculture. Cutting soil emissions cuts overall greenhouse gas emissions, and regenerative practices can act as natural carbon dioxide removal.

soil-env-194.title: Engineering with living plants
soil-env-194.text: Some of the sturdiest slope defenses are alive. Soil bioengineering uses living plant materials, from seeds to whole plant communities, for engineering jobs such as stabilizing slopes and controlling erosion. A discipline of civil engineering, it sometimes replaces classical works but more often complements them. Used for many centuries and promoted with European examples by Schiechtl in 1980, it is now practiced worldwide on eroding slopes and embankments. Plantings shield soil from wind, rain, frost and flowing water. They slow flow along banks, bind soil, trap snow, sand and sediment, and roughen slopes against avalanches. Their roots loosen soil, and they improve the water regime, even out temperatures and enrich raw soils. They also heal scars left by landslides, wildfires, mining and construction. The method works wherever its plants grow well, from tropical to temperate zones. It is limited in arid, frost, alpine and arctic regions and in species-poor areas. It is not always cheaper to build. Over its lifetime, though, it is normally more economical, because the works become living systems that maintain themselves by succession.

soil-env-183.title: Maps that show what a soil can do
soil-env-183.text: A soil map can show more than soil types. Soil mapping identifies, describes and delineates those types from field observation or from inferences drawn from sources such as aerial photographs. Mapping soil functions goes further, turning properties into interpretations for a purpose: food production, environmental protection or civil engineering. A map may show one property, such as critical nutrient or heavy-metal levels, or a combined interpretation such as an erosion risk index. The method extends soil survey, pairing maps of soil components with pedotransfer functions and soil inference models to infer how mapping units will perform.

soil-env-182.title: Soil as the land's filter and buffer
soil-env-182.text: Water that passes through soil comes out cleaner. Soil particles capture contaminants, so what reaches aquifers and rivers carries less of them. This is one of soil's functions: regulating water, and filtering, buffering and transforming materials that move between the atmosphere, plant cover and water table. Soil also transforms and decomposes waste materials into new materials. And it can store large amounts of carbon as soil organic matter, which lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide and helps mitigate climate change.

soil-env-195.title: How a drain field lets soil microbes clean wastewater
soil-env-195.text: Sewage leaving a {{ref:soil-env-216}} still needs cleaning, and soil finishes the job. A septic drain field, or leach field, is a subsurface facility that removes contaminants from that liquid. It usually has trenches of perforated pipe and porous material, often gravel, covered with soil to keep animals and surface runoff away. The tank is sized for anaerobic organisms, which live without oxygen. The field is sized for aerobic soil microbes, which turn the tank's anaerobic effluent into aerobic water. A biofilm on the trench walls uses atmospheric oxygen to break down organic compounds. Incomplete oxidation shows as hydrogen sulfide odors or iron bacteria in nearby wells. Design is hydraulic, for wastewater volume, and catabolic, for its long-term biochemical oxygen demand. The microbes barely touch petroleum products and chlorinated solvents and cannot remove dissolved metals. Bleach or sanitizers can slow or stop them. Fields with several areas let one rest while nematodes eat built-up biofilm and fats, though percolation rarely regains its first clean-water rate. A biofilter lowers the effluent's oxygen demand, not its volume, so the field can be smaller.

soil-env-216.title: The septic tank: sewage treatment in a buried chamber
soil-env-216.text: In 2008 about 20 percent of US households relied on a septic tank. It is an underground chamber of concrete, fiberglass or plastic where household sewage gets primary treatment. Solids settle and are digested without oxygen in the first chamber. The liquid flows to a septic drain field, whose soil must pass a percolation test. Sludge outpaces decomposition, so a vacuum truck removes it every few years, or every 10-20 years in some systems. Tanks remove little nitrogen. Soils usually retain phosphorus, but sandy soils near water can saturate and pass it on, risking {{ref:soil-env-020}}. Dense development can push groundwater pollution past acceptable limits.

soil-env-196.title: Will this soil take septic effluent?
soil-env-196.text: A drain field site must be permeable enough for effluent to percolate away, yet fine enough to hold back disease-causing bacteria and viruses. Aerobic conditions must kill those pathogens before they reach wells or surface water. Sand and gravel pass wastewater too fast; silt and clay limit flow. A percolation test times clean water dispersing from a trench. Where seasonal high water tables limit sizing, a soil scientist reads the soil's morphology instead. Texture, structure, pores and the color signatures of a fluctuating water table all count. In service, biofilm, fine particles, congealed fats, rising groundwater and frozen ground clog the trench's soil interface, and percolation falls.

soil-env-217.title: Putting a mined landscape back together
soil-env-217.text: An open-cut mine is refilled in layers. Rock backfills the pit, then stored pre-mining soil, topsoil and vegetation. This is mine reclamation: modifying mined land so it is ecologically functional or economically usable again. The original landscape cannot always return. Usually the limit is how far mine waste can be physically and chemically stabilized. The Forestry Reclamation Approach calls for a loosely graded, uncompacted rooting layer at least four feet deep, of topsoil or weathered sandstone. In the United States, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 makes operators file a reclamation plan and a bond before mining. A coal tax funds abandoned-mine reclamation.

soil-env-197.title: India's soil health cards for millions of farmers
soil-env-197.text: By 16 May 2017, India had distributed 725 lakh soil health cards. The Soil Health Card Scheme, launched on 19 February 2015, gives farmers cards with crop-wise nutrient and fertilizer advice based on soil tests. Experts flag micronutrient deficiencies, and balanced fertilizer use should raise yields at lower cost. The government allocated ₹568 crore (US$61 million), and the 2016 Union budget added ₹100 crore (US$11 million). By July 2015 only 34 lakh cards had been issued, against a 2015–16 target of 84 lakh. It followed Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006, credited with helping the state's farm growth reach three times the national rate in 2009.

soil-env-191.title: Europe's unfinished soil law
soil-env-191.text: The European Union treats soil as a non-renewable resource, yet leaves its governance largely to member states. A 2006 European Commission proposal for a soil protection framework would have unified scattered EU rules. Member states rejected it under the subsidiarity principle, arguing that their own strong soil policies sufficed. The EU still has no cohesive soil governance policy. Under the European Green Deal, the EU Soil Strategy for 2030, launched in 2021, aims at healthy soils for food security and climate mitigation. Its Soil Monitoring Law was first meant to be legally binding on soil health; the final version set no obligatory targets and covers only monitoring.

soil-env-190.title: A worldwide partnership for limited soils
soil-env-190.text: In December 2012 the FAO and its members set up the Global Soil Partnership to govern the planet's limited soils better. Its goal is food security and restored ecosystem services, by conserving, enhancing and restoring soils through productive, sustainable use. Membership is open and voluntary. FAO member countries work with universities, research centres, soil science societies, UN agencies, NGOs, companies, farmer associations and donors, through Regional Soil Partnerships. Its First Plenary Assembly, at FAO headquarters in June 2013, set up the Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils. The panel's 27 experts from all regions advise on science and advocate sustainable soil management.

soil-env-192.title: Soil policy in a nation of farmers
soil-env-192.text: In 2010 agriculture employed 58.2% of India's workforce and contributed 15.7% of its GDP. India's soil policy is shaped by that weight and by widespread farmland degradation. Excessive, miscalculated fertilizer use aimed at higher output has left nearly two-thirds of India's farmland classed as degraded or sick. Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006 tested farmers' soil and advised on fertilizer and crops. The Ministry of Agriculture later extended it nationwide. India's National Programme to Combat Desertification builds capacity in soil and water management, micro-credit for women and marginalized groups, alternative energy, and land laws for industry and mining.

soil-env-193.title: Guarding soils in cities and industrial zones
soil-env-193.text: In the developing world, industrialization and urbanization are emerging as major causes of soil degradation. Industry alters soil chemistry with heavy metals and effluents. Construction and landfills compact and excavate soil, disturbing how it purifies and stores water. Poor knowledge of soil management and disregard for the environment drive the damage. Developing countries often lack the resources to enforce policies, leaving soil and water heavily polluted. Urban soil management takes an interdisciplinary approach. It protects soil-dependent biodiversity, reduces industrial pollution and makes soil more resilient to construction compaction. In Central Europe, networks of universities and municipal authorities design soil strategies for selected cities.

openers.soil-health-and-protection: Soil can be worn out, and it can be rebuilt. Poor management degrades it in four general ways: erosion, and physical, chemical and biological decline. To know how far a soil has slipped, scientists judge its health and quality with physical, chemical and biological measurements, sometimes against native land nearby. Repair comes through regenerative farming methods, many drawn from conservation agriculture. It also comes through the policies and decisions that nation states and local governments apply to soil.

reviews.soil-health-and-protection: Soil health proved to be a matter of perspective as well as measurement. Users weigh soil functions differently, so tests, indicators and native-land benchmarks all chase a moving target. The threats are clearer: erosion, compaction, pollution and fertilizer that suppresses soil microbes, which have cost soils an estimated 133 billion tonnes of carbon since farming began. Regeneration answers with less tillage, cover crops, amendments and living plants on unstable slopes, while drain fields show soil cleaning wastewater every day. Because soil forms over thousands of years and human change is fast, governance matters, from World Soil Day to India's soil health cards and Europe's unfinished soil law.
